sentence: I would say that, in addition to the operating efficiencies, advertising is also starting to make an impact on gross profit, although advertising is smaller in the international segment than it is in North America, it's growing at a same rapid clip year over year.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Even while in International we're continuing to invest in a lot of areas, we continue to front-load Prime benefits for the newer geographies, we continue to launch new countries -- we launched Prime in Australia recently.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We've launched devices in multiple countries: Echo and Alexa were launched in France, Echo Spot was launched in India and Japan in the last quarter.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So it's a mix of operating efficiencies as we grow, and then also continuing to invest on a lot of fronts.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Our next question comes from Mark Mahaney with RBC Capital Markets.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Hey, maybe two things.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Just a little bit of color on that unit growth, I think, it was 17%, any particular things to call out there as that would have stunted that growth or negatively limited?

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Or is that just kind of the new, new normal?

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: And then, Brian, I'm sorry, you just talked better-than-expected efficiencies in operations, could I ask you to tease that out a little bit more, and a little more color particularly on the retail side of the business?

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Are there particular newfound efficiencies that are sustainable?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Let's start with unit growth.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So I will note, we did a very strong unit growth rate last year in Q2, with 27%, so we're comping against that.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: As we look back on that, there were a number of factors.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I mean, in any quarter there can be product mix or ASP differentials which shift the unit growth figure but if you also remember, we dropped our Super Saver Shipping threshold twice, the early part of last year from $49 to $35; and then down to $25.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So there was a bit of growth, particularly in lower ASP items from that that we saw last year.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we're comping that.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Another factor is digital content that moves to subscription.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So Amazon Music and Kindle Unlimited, while they're very successful and it's a good transition, the units do not count in this unit calculation.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So there are some things like that, that maybe obfuscate the numbers a bit but we're really pleased with the retail growth.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We think it's driven by again Prime, the Prime program, the engagement of Prime customers as well as the increased selection, and particularly third-party selection.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: On operations, if you look at probably the last 18 months, you're going to see a lot of different pace of increase in both infrastructure costs and capital costs, and the addition of fixed cost heads.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So one thing that you'll notice is that we've stepped down our rate of growth of fixed headcount, excluding the acquisitions, we've grown 26% year over year at the end of June, on a trailing 12-month basis but 23% of that was in the second half of last year.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we are continuing to look at where we're investing headcount.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We're seeing a lot of our growth areas being fueled by headcount that's moving within the company.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: There's a lot of movement of tech headcount.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And so there was less external hiring in the first half of this year.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We don't think that that's necessarily the long-term trend but it certainly created a lot of operating efficiencies, and now we'll reset and evaluate where we need to still add people.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So I think the first half of the year could be a good test of where our cost structure is, coming off of the investment that leads up to the holiday.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Last year, there was a lot of first-half investment.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: If you look back on infrastructure and fixed headcount that may be made that less pronounced but this year it's a little more apparent.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Our next question comes from the line of Douglas Anmuth with J.P.Morgan.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Douglas Anmuth
sentence: Thanks for taking the question.

speaker: Douglas Anmuth
sentence: Wanted to ask two, if I could.

speaker: Douglas Anmuth
sentence: First, 3Q is typically a heavy fulfillment center build-out period ahead of the holidays, and then lower utilization but obviously your profit outlook is good.

speaker: Douglas Anmuth
sentence: Can you just give us a sense of how you're thinking about FC build out and square footage increases this year?

speaker: Douglas Anmuth
sentence: And then, secondly a lot of excitement around the pharmacy opportunity with the acquisition of PillPack.

speaker: Douglas Anmuth
sentence: Can you frame some of the strategic rationale there around the acquisition, and how that helps advance your efforts, and how we should think about integration going forward?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: On the fulfillment center capacity, I don't have a number for you, today.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I'll probably clarify that at the end of next quarter as we head into holiday but if you think back, the last two years, we've added square footage that's exceeded 30% growth, both in 2016 and 2017.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We anticipate it's going to be lower this year as we get some efficiencies off what we've built over the last few years but I don't have a number for you today.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I will say that the majority of it is being put in service in the back-end of the year, just like in the last two years but we'll clarify that next quarter.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: On PillPack, yes, the deal, of course, hasn't closed, yet.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We expect to close it in the second half of the year, so I'll limit my comments right now but we're excited.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I think the company has a really highly differentiated customer experience, and they've done a great job getting to the size and scale that they're at today.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We think that working together with them we can expand on that in the future.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: They're like a lot of the other acquisitions we've done.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Recently, we're looking for well-run companies with highly differentiated customer experience, and a real sense of customer obsession that matches ours.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we think PillPack has got all those traits, and we look forward to the deal closing and working with them.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Our next question comes from Mark May with Citi.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Mark May
sentence: On AWS, does the backlog there give you confidence in the ability for this business to continue to post the type of robust growth that you've seen of late?

speaker: Mark May
sentence: And on Alexa, now that you're reaching a meaningful number of Alexa users, I wondered if you could discuss a bit more about how Alexa is impacting retail business?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Let me start with AWS.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Yeah, we're very happy with the results we're seeing, and the backlog that we see, and the new contracts and new customers and the expansion of existing customer business that we see.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Again, the business has accelerated the last three quarters, and we're seeing great signs in a number of areas.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We've added 800 new services and features so far this year; that's an accelerated pace from last year, which was a record year.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We see customers have migrated more than 80,000 databases using the AWS Database Migration Service.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And customers are just branching out to a lot of new products from us.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: There are new areas like machine learning, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, serverless computing and database and analytics are really big.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we think that when you look at it, why do people come to us?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: It's essentially set functionality and pace of innovation that we've demonstrated for multiple years.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We've built a very strong partner and customer ecosystem.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And frankly we have the most proven reliability of security and performance, and we've been at this longer than anyone else.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So, again, we continue to deliver for customers.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We continue to use feedback from customers to develop new services and features.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: The operating margin itself will fluctuate quarter to quarter, a very strong performance this quarter.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Obviously, part of that was in the capital leases being flat year over year, and the team's ability to really run the data centers at a higher efficiency.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: And I think, the second question was just related to how is Alexa impacting the business, overall.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Hey, this is Dave.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: I think we're having a lot of success with devices and customers are enjoying those.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: We talked to coming out of Prime Day, had some good success and happy customers enjoying some of the devices there.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So, I think, the focus now is really having a good and exciting roadmap of recent revises and more to come ahead, and getting those into customers' hands.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Our next question comes from the line of Heath Terry with Goldman Sachs.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Heath Terry
sentence: Just on the AWS point, as you're seeing customers to AWS, you're adding new customers to AWS, can you give us a sense of sort of where you're seeing customers spend focus.

speaker: Heath Terry
sentence: You mentioned database but what other areas you're potentially seeing as customers move up the stack with you and grow?

speaker: Heath Terry
sentence: And then, you flagged the flat capital lease growth on a year-over-year basis.

speaker: Heath Terry
sentence: In the past when you've talked about the growth in capex and capital lease, you generally referred to trying to grow those numbers or that infrastructure growth overall more or less with the business.

speaker: Heath Terry
sentence: Is there some level of efficiency breakthrough that you've gotten there where that's no longer the case?

speaker: Heath Terry
sentence: Or is it a function of timing?

speaker: Heath Terry
sentence: How should we think about what that capex and capital lease spend signals about your expectations for growth?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I would say it's just a demonstration of the very tight period where we've still added a lot, I mean, $4.6 billion is a lot of capital leases but the rate of growth over last year is flat.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So what I would say is, I'm not sure about the breakthrough element of it.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We do spend a lot of time driving better efficiency in our data centers.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We do see it; sometimes it is higher than other quarters.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: The starting point for our expectation would be that our growth in infrastructure costs would start with the growth in usage, which has been exceeding the revenue growth rate but we can drive more efficiently and we can sometimes bank the efficiencies of prior investments that we've made in other periods.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So it will fluctuate quarter to quarter.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I would say last year in the first half was a pretty large investment area.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I'll lump it in with capital expenditures but in the first two quarters, Q1 of last year, it was 82% growth year over year in capital expenditures, Q2 was 67%.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: This year, those numbers are 33% in Q1, and 1% in Q2.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So there's a bit of timing at play here but I think overall, in the longer-term, we certainly work to drive efficiency in both AWS infrastructure capability and also in our warehouse networks.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I don't have on the other piece, on product detail, I don't have anything more for you.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I would just say that, our growth is coming from customers that span from start-ups to enterprise customers to government agencies, and they start small and then they continue to build and shift their businesses to us, and a large number have gone all-in on AWS, and have had a chance to lower their cost structures as a result.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I'd count Amazon in that category because on the consumer side of the business, we increasingly see infrastructure savings due to the conversion to AWS resources.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Our next question comes from Brian Nowak with Morgan Stanley.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Brian Nowak
sentence: Thanks for taking my questions, I have two.

speaker: Brian Nowak
sentence: The first one on the ad business, Brian, I was just wondering, could you give us some examples of some products you've had particular success with on the ad side?

speaker: Brian Nowak
sentence: And I know you guys are always focused on removing customer friction points and solving pain points for customers, maybe talk to us about some of the still existing pain points for your advertiser customers you're looking to address with the advertising product?

speaker: Brian Nowak
sentence: And the second one, I know it's an accounting question but we're going to be asked it a lot.

speaker: Brian Nowak
sentence: On revenue accounting, can you just sort of walk us through any of the accounting changes that any of the revenue lines had in the current quarter because of the multiple accounting moving pieces?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Yeah, let me give Dave a chance afterward to talk about that piece but I'll start with advertising.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So conceptually stepping back, it's now a multibillion-dollar business for us.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We're seeing strong adoption across a number of fronts.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Amazon vendors, sellers, authors as well as third-party advertisers who want to reach Amazon customers.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we have hundreds of thousands of emerging and established advertisers.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And they're using our services to achieve their marketing goals, whether that's to drive new brand awareness, discovery or ultimately purchase decisions on our site.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Pain points and improvements, I would say, our priorities include improving the usability of our tools for advertisers, helping make smarter recommendations for customers.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Automating, we're doing a lot of work on automating the activities that the advertisers need to do, and continue to invent new products for those advertisers.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We also think measurement is going to be important so we're focused on our measurement capabilities, so advertisers understand what outcomes they're driving on our properties.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And we think that we're uniquely positioned to show them the direct benefit of their advertising.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: And Brian, this is Dave.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Just on the accounting piece, specifically to Q2, the impact of the Accounting Standards Update, revenue-recognition changes we did starting in the first part of the year, it's a $640 million increase to other revenue, specifically related to how we treat some of the advertising services.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So you remember as part of the adoption beginning in 2018, certainly, the advertising services were classified as revenue rather than the cost of sales.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So $640 million more is in other revenue this second quarter.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: You'd see that in that line item, which is about $2.2 billion here in the second quarter.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: In addition to that, some of the other factors I talked about last quarter, some of the treatment of gross to net changes in some sales of apps and app content, digital media costs, some of that shift created a headwind for online stores revenue.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So that year-over-year growth rate for that line item would have been higher but for that change.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Our next question comes from Eric Sheridan with UBS.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: Two questions if I can.

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: On Whole Foods, any update on the integration of Whole Foods within the broader Prime ecosystem, the way in which you're tying those assets and customer bases together to sort of promote the flywheel that you've talked about a fair bit?

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: And Prime Now, any update on the scale of markets globally, and what you're learning as Prime Now continues to scale in terms of how users adopt the service, putting SKUs closer to prem what that does to the velocity of purchasing?

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: Thank you so much.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So, it was a big quarter for Whole Foods and Prime.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We launched additional savings for Prime members at Whole Foods.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: If you go to Whole Foods store or Whole Foods Market 365 store, you see a lot of yellow stickers for 10% discounts on hundreds of sale items.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: You also see deep discounts on selected popular products.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So Prime members have adopted this benefit, it's one of the fastest rates we've ever seen for a Prime benefit, and they've already saved millions of dollars on everything from seasonal favorites to, as I said, popular daily sales.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So in addition, we've expanded grocery delivery to 20 cities so that's picking up steam.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: During the Prime Day, we had some unique deals for Prime customers at Whole Foods.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Actually, the deals lasted for a week at Whole Foods.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And people had, again the ability to see the benefit that Prime membership saves incremental dollars, because of it at Whole Foods.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And the Prime Rewards Visa Card, which gives you 5% off on all purchases has been applied to Whole Foods' purchases as well.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So that is the second wave, probably after the first wave where we talked in previous calls about initial price drops, putting lockers in the stores, selling some of the Whole Foods' products on the Amazon site, and other things.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So the invention level is still really high.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We think it's a big milestone this quarter to launch Prime benefits with Whole Foods, and we'll keep going, we'll see how that develops.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I guess, my comments are that it's in 50 cities worldwide, it's across 9 countries.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We have multiple options for you in grocery delivery.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We have the delivery services, so AmazonFresh and Prime Now which serve a certain need.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We have a traditional grocery store now with Whole Foods, and then we have the combination of those two with home delivery, and we're using Prime Now or Whole Foods products through Prime Now to make those deliveries, as well as the new kind of stores with Amazon Go that we're experimenting with.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So lots of innovation, invention on that front as well.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Our next question comes from Ross Sandler with Barclays.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Ross Sandler
sentence: Hey guys, I had two questions.

speaker: Ross Sandler
sentence: First is on the Music business.

speaker: Ross Sandler
sentence: So I think, you said recently you had tens of millions of paying subscribers.

speaker: Ross Sandler
sentence: So are those paying music listeners coming from Prime, and using the mobile app, are they coming in from Echo?

speaker: Ross Sandler
sentence: Any color on what's driving that uptake and converting users into paid members?

speaker: Ross Sandler
sentence: Then the second question is, you mentioned efficiency gains in retail and the improvement in retail operating margin.

speaker: Ross Sandler
sentence: If we look at International, it's still negative but it's also improving pretty meaningfully, so can you parse where that improvement's coming from between India and the other emerging markets versus some of the more mature markets in Western Europe?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Sure, let me start with that second question.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So, yes, we have seen over the last few quarters, improved operating margins internationally.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I would say in places like Europe and Japan, we're seeing many of the efficiencies I talked about earlier on the fixed headcount, operations costs, infrastructure costs, and also things like marketing working to be very efficient.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: I would also say that, although it's smaller internationally the impact of advertising is starting to show up more and more internationally.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: It's growing quite quickly just as it is in North America but you're right, we continue to invest.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We're investing in India obviously, and have seen good traction there.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We just celebrated our Fifth Year Anniversary as the most visited site in India.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we think there's a lot of great innovation that has continued to occur for Indian consumers and sellers, and that will continue but you're also seeing additional expansion.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we launched Prime in Australia; we're rolling devices out.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We launched Echo and Alexa in France.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: The Echo Spot in India and Japan, and we announced that we're going to expand Echo and Alexa soon to Italy, Mexico and Spain.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So I would say that we're continuing to frontload Prime benefits in the newer geographies.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So that's one of the issues that we see with operating margin but we think it's the right thing to do.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We are seeing strong traction in that front as well.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We also like that the on Prime Day, we were able to expand our list of countries that experience Prime Day; this year to Australia, Singapore, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So we're very bullish on our International business.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We do realize it's a period of investment and we're in different stages of growth in different countries.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Yeah, and this is Dave.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Just quickly on Music, as you mentioned, tens of millions of paid customers are enjoying Amazon Music.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: When you look at the Amazon Music Unlimited subscription, it continues to grow very quickly.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: We've got those offerings in more than 30 countries now and the catalog there's tens of millions of songs, and a lot of rich playlists, personalized stations, those kinds of things.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Of course, we started in Music with Prime Music, a little bit earlier in that space, and I think that's been a great way for Prime members to enjoy some of that catalog for free, and then as they enjoy that, be able to move into the Amazon Music Unlimited skill.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: One of the great things that are also part of that, I think, you alluded to it is just Alexa, and one of the most popular features we see as you probably imagine for using those devices are just interacting with Alexa, wherever you may be is being able to listen to music.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So that's proven to be a, I think, a good skill for folks to be able to enjoy in addition to a really kind of rich and growing Amazon skill set.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: We now have more than 45,000 skills available to customers.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Our next question comes from Youssef Squali with SunTrust Robinson Humphrey.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Youssef Squali
sentence: Thank you very much.

speaker: Youssef Squali
sentence: On the new Supreme Court decision, you guys have been collecting state taxes in all 45 states where it's applicable for a 1P. And for a 3P, I think, it was in two states.

speaker: Youssef Squali
sentence: Have you seen any slowdown to growth in these two states since you began collecting taxes?

speaker: Youssef Squali
sentence: I think you started maybe last 12 months or so.

speaker: Youssef Squali
sentence: When will you start collecting taxes in the rest of the country, and will you charge for it?

speaker: Youssef Squali
sentence: Because my understanding is that, in those two states you do not collect or you do not charge to help these 3P sellers file taxes or collect state taxes.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Hey, Youssef, this is Dave.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So, right now, as you mentioned 45 states that have a state-imposed sales tax, first-party products we do our own collection on that.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: For 3P sellers right now, it's three states.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So Washington State started as of January 1, Pennsylvania as of April 1, and most recently Oklahoma on July 1.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So those are the ones where we're collecting and remitting.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: And to your second point, we've not talked about any kind of trends.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: As you could imagine some of these are still really early days.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Our final question comes from Jason Helfstein with Oppenheimer & Company.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Please proceed with your question.

speaker: Jason Helfstein
sentence: Given the focus in the press release about Alexa Voice Services, any thoughts about how you would monetize on third-party devices?

speaker: Jason Helfstein
sentence: And then just a follow up on Amazon Prime Video Channels, any plans to offer standard skinny bundles to become a cable replacement?

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: Yeah, let me start with Alexa.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So right now, our emphasis is around expanding the reach of Alexa and the usefulness.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So as Dave mentioned, we're now up over 45,000 skills.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We have a developer network that's expanded and we have over 13,000 smart home devices from 2,500 unique brands.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: You're seeing things like expansion into the hotel space where we're partnering with hotels to allow you to experience Alexa while you're traveling.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: And you saw from the quote that was in our press release from Jeff, the number of Alexa-enabled devices has tripled in the past year including some really large companies like Polk, Sonos, Acer, Hewlett-Packard, Lenovo, BMW, Ford, Toyota to name a few.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So that's the biggest emphasis, is getting the expansion of Alexa to places where it can be useful.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We also are developing new machine learning tools to help developers more easily build Alexa skills.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: We feel like we're getting great traction there.

speaker: Brian Olsavsky
sentence: So I think your original question was about monetization of Alexa but right now the biggest thing we can do is to make it as useful as possible and make devices that can use the skills.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Yeah, and then just on the second question.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: I mean, I can't speculate on what we might do in the future but I'd say today, with Prime Channels, I think, we're really pleased with the growth we're seeing.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: We've seen some good channels come online over the last few quarters, and seen some good traction there.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So we'll keep focusing on building out an even better selection because it's clear to us that customers want that option to be able to add that content as part of their Prime memberships.

sentence: Joining us today to answer your questions is Brian Olsavsky, our CFO; and Dave Fildes, Director of Investor Relations.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: As you listen to today's conference call, we encourage you to have our press release in front of you, which includes our financial results as well as metrics and commentary on the quarter.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: Please note, unless otherwise stated, all comparisons in this call will be against our results for the comparable period of 2018.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: Our comments and responses to your questions reflect Management's views as of today April 25, 2019 only and will include forward-looking statements.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: Actual results may differ materially.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: Additional information about factors that could potentially impact our financial results is included in today's press release and our filings with the SEC, including our most recent annual report on Form 10-K and subsequent filings.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: During this call, we may discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: In our press release, slides accompanying this webcast and our filings with the SEC, each of which is posted on our IR website, you will find additional disclosures regarding these non-GAAP measures, including reconciliations of these measures with comparable GAAP measures.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: Our guidance incorporates the order trends that we've seen to-date and what we believe today to be appropriate assumptions.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: Our results are inherently unpredictable and may be materially affected by many factors, including fluctuations in foreign exchange rates, changes in global economic conditions and customer spending, world events, the rate of growth of the Internet, online commerce and cloud services and the various factors detailed in our filings with the SEC.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: Our guidance also assumes among other things that we don't conclude any additional business acquisitions, investments, restructurings or legal settlements.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: It's not possible to accurately predict demand for our goods and services and therefore our actual results could differ materially from our guidance.

speaker: Shelly Kay Pfeiffer
sentence: With that, we will move to Q&A. Operator, please remind our listeners how to initiate a question.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: I'm going to ask two questions because the first one is really simple.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Unit growth of 10%, is this a meaningless metric?

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Just talk through that number.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: I think it's the lowest unit growth I think we've ever seen, but just talk to us a little bit about that.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: And then international sales growth decelerated 16%.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: I know last ex-FX, I know last quarter you talked about some challenges in the India market.

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Just give us some color please around that growth rate, how do we think about the sustainability of that?

speaker: Mark Mahaney
sentence: Was that negatively impacted by developments in India?

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Thanks for your questions.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: I'll start on unit growth.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So unit growth was 10%.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Again, as I mentioned last quarter, this measurement excludes a lot of our fastest growing businesses, things like AWS, advertising, subscription services, which cannibalize the unit calculation, things like Kindle Unlimited and Amazon Music Unlimited.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And also, it doesn't include Whole Foods Market.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So -- while it is meaningful, it needs to be understood and caveated.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So your second question was on international growth.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Yeah, talking more about specifically India.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So India for those of you on the call last quarter, we were just heading into an uncertain period with the PN2 ruling.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We did make some changes to our structure to stay in compliance with all regulations.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: There was a few days of downtime for some of our selection.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: But for the full quarter, the impact was minimal and we're in compliance and we're very happy with the progress of the business in India.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So as far as the growth is concerned in international, we had some noise in Q3 and Q4, if you remember, with the timing of the Diwali holiday, but we feel pretty good about the Q1 growth there, even despite some downtime in India.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Our next question comes from the line of Doug Anmuth from JPMorgan.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: You are now live.

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: Thanks for taking the questions.

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: I'll also ask two, if I could.

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: Just first Brian, can you just talk about the outperformance in operating income in 1Q?

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: Pretty significant beat there.

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: Looks like cost of sales and fulfillment, but hoping you can provide some more color.

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: And then why would the margin be materially lower in Q2 as you're guiding?

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: And then just second on the outlook for revenue in the second quarter on an FX-neutral basis, the higher end implies a nice acceleration.

speaker: Doug Anmuth
sentence: So curious what gives you the confidence in that.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Yeah, let's start with Q1.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So you remember last quarter I made the point that 2018 saw lower growth in some of our key cost areas, things like fulfillment capacity which had been growing over 30% a year in 2016 and '17, dropped to 15% last year.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Headcount growth was 48% in 2016, 38% if you exclude Whole Foods and Souq acquisitions in 2017.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: That dropped to 14% last year.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And then financial leases for infrastructure, which are good proxy for our capital investment and infrastructure, after growing 69% in 2017, grew 10%.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So all of those trailing 12-month metrics actually stayed the same or slightly declined in Q1.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we had continued efficiency.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We didn't put a lot of new fulfillment center capacity or infrastructure into place, at least compared to Q1 of last year.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And hiring was moderate.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We actually were down to 12% on a trailing 12-month basis.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So I would say that is a continuation of last year.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: But my point from the last call still holds in that, we do expect those growth rates to be higher for all of 2019.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So most of that will happen in the next three quarters and we have that built into the Q2 guidance.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And we also hit the high end of the revenue range, which is always good from efficiency standpoint and the drop through on the higher end of the revenue.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So now turning into Q2, I would like to tell you a bit about why that's lower.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we have -- we're currently working on evolving our Prime free two-day shipping program to be a free one-day shipping program.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We're able to do this because we've spent 20-plus years expanding our fulfillment and logistics network, but this is still a big investment and a lot of work to do ahead of us.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: For Q2 guidance, we've included approximately $800 million of incremental spend related to this investment.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And just to clarify to give a little more information, we have been offering obviously faster than two-day shipping for Prime members for years.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: One-day, same day even down to one- to two-hour delivery for Prime Now.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we're going to continue to do to offer same-day and Prime Now selection on accelerated basis, but this is all about the core free two-day offer morphing into -- or evolving into a free one-day offer.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We've already started down this path.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We've, in the past month, significantly expanded our one-day eligible selection and also expanded the number of zip codes eligible for one-day shipping.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we're taking a significant step.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: It wasn't showing up in Q1, it was minimal in Q2 -- in Q1's results.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: It's a significant step and it will take us time to achieve and we want to ensure that we have a good delivery experience for our customers as we evolve the software.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And lastly I would say in Q2 as a reminder, each year we -- it's -- Q2 is the time when we grant RSUs to employees and we traditionally see a step up in stock-based compensation expense in Q2.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And we're seeing the same thing this year.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And that's also tied in with your question about revenue acceleration.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We do believe that although there's not explicit lift built in for the faster shipping, we have seen good order trends to -- month-to-date and we expect -- we built the Q2 range about -- around what we've seen.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Our next question is from Justin Post from Merrill Lynch.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: You are now live.

speaker: Justin Post
sentence: As users consume more services and maybe get less boxes, although I guess you could see a pick up in Q2, what does that mean for customer stickiness?

speaker: Justin Post
sentence: How are you thinking about getting more advertising and getting more subscription services?

speaker: Justin Post
sentence: And maybe if you could just give us a little insight into what you're seeing with Prime churn, especially in the more mature US market?

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Justin, I would stay, as I said I believe on the last call, we had more people sign up for Prime in 2018 than any other year before.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we are very happy with the -- not only the absolute membership levels of the Prime program, but also the engagement.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Our engagement in video benefit -- or excuse me, Prime benefits shipping, hours watched on video, hours listened to on music, all of them are trending in the right direction and continue to get more and more sticky.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So while I can't share -- I won't share with you today the Prime -- any Prime -- specific Prime statistics about churn, it does remain a very compelling program.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: I think the announcement I just made about morphing to a one-day free shipping offer will make it even more the best deal in retail as we say.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Our next question comes from Eric Sheridan from UBS.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Your are now live.

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: Thanks for taking the question.

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: The advertising business saw, what looks like, a little bit of a step down again in Q1 versus Q4.

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: Q4 was a fairly big step down when you strip out the accounting benefit or the last quarter of the accounting benefit.

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: Can you talk a little bit about the supply and demand dynamics in the advertising business?

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: How much of that will you might be controlling to make some decisions about ad load versus the demand to advertise among sellers on the platform?

speaker: Eric Sheridan
sentence: And any color you could give us on what you might be seeing in the advertising business domestically versus internationally would be helpful?

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We're seeing, as you can see in the operating margin, we're seeing good advertising growth both in North America and also internationally.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: While I can't get into some of the questions about ad loads and inventory, I would say really what we're focused on right now is driving relevancy and ensuring that we surface the most useful ads possible.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: I think that's going to be the best experience for customers and also for advertisers.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So most of our focus has been on, again, adding more functionality, adding more products and adding reporting for businesses and advertisers, so they can understand the incremental customers they're seeing on Amazon through advertising with Amazon.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So it's more right now about tools and making better recommendations, making it easier to use Amazon demand side platform, things like that, operational improvements.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And then, I guess, we're very focused on serving brands as well.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: That's another theme that we have.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: This -- brand stores that we have are easy to create, customize and we've had great pickup on that from brands for they can show shoppers who they are and tell their story.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So it builds a better engagement for the brand and the customer, it builds better customer loyalty both to that brand and also to Amazon.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And then on the brand side itself, we have new reporting, excuse me, where we're again looking to measure the new to the brand shoppers and what lift they're seeing.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So I would say right now, it's more about efficiency and also performance of the advertisements themselves.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: The other revenue growth that you see does include some non-advertising things as well.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So while other revenue grew 36% and it is principally advertising, advertising grew a bit higher than that.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Our next question is from Stephen Ju from Credit Suisse.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: You are now live.

speaker: Stephen Ju
sentence: You can share in regards to the Prime users' awareness of the availability of stuff from Whole Foods.

speaker: Stephen Ju
sentence: Is the order flow coming in from a wide number of users or is the activity coming in from a small, but a very dedicated number of customers?

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Thanks, Stephen.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: I would say that we're very -- it's widespread and more Prime members have adopted the Whole Foods benefit than almost any other benefit we've offered them and they're saving as a result hundreds of millions of dollars.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We continue to expand the coverage for delivery.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We have delivery from 75 -- in 75 US metros through the Prime Now app and we also have pickup in over 30 metros, also through the Prime Now app.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we're very -- the other, excuse me, the other point I'll make is just like last quarter, I'll remind you that the physical stores revenue is principally Whole Foods revenue, but it excludes the online ordering component, where people order on the Prime Now app and it's delivered to them.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: That shows up in our online stores classification.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So last quarter, I told you that our growth in store sales including both shopping and also online deliveries was closer to 6% in Q4 and it's a similar number in Q1.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So again, we're very happy with both the Prime adoption of -- or the recognition of the Prime benefits by -- at Whole Foods and also the purchases.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And you may have also noticed that we lowered prices for the third major round of price cuts since we joined forces with Whole Foods in the summer of 2017.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Our next question is from Dan Salmon from BMO Capital Markets.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: You are now live.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: Good afternoon, everyone.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: Maybe Brian just to return to the advertising business for a moment.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: It does sound like as Eric noted that there was a bit more of a slowdown again.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: I mean, I guess, I'll ask it this way.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: Do you believe that some of the improved relevance, some of the improved focus on brands as well as some of the new products can lead that business to reaccelerate at some point again or is it facing law of large numbers?

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: And then just a follow up, just to return to the $800 million investment to improve one-day shipping, it sounds like that investment is under way already and that in noting that it'll help contribute to the high end of the guidance this quarter.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: It sounds like the timing of that is fairly quicker.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: I would imagine it's just simply expanding availability and that that $800 million is largely related to shipping costs.

speaker: Dan Salmon
sentence: But I just want to make sure understanding that quickly that the -- this investment rolled out relatively quickly and starts to take effect relatively quickly.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: I'm glad you asked that.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: I would say that while our 20-year head start in investments in logistics and fulfillment capacity and partner networks that we've built are helping us, we also do have a network that is tuned to two-day delivery right now, principally for two-day delivery.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we do need to build out more one-day capacity along with our transportation partners, but we're moving quickly and we've got a good head start.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: There is a certain tranche that we can dial up quickly and we've started to do that and you'll see that very quickly in Q2.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And then stay tuned because we'll be building this -- most of this capacity through the year in 2019.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And then your question about advertising, I wouldn't comment on acceleration or deceleration of growth.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: I would just say we're early on in this venture, there's a lot of -- it's having a lot of pickup by both vendors, sellers and also authors.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So again, we feel like if we work on the inputs in this business and continue to grow traffic to the site, we will have a good outcome in the advertising space.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Operator Our next question is from Anthony DiClemente from Evercore.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: You are now live.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: Thanks very much.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: A couple of questions.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: On the shareholder letter, Jeff wrote third-party sellers are kicking our first-party butt and we read through that.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: But as we kind of look at the trending and the pacing of the 3P business, you can see a little bit of a deceleration in the 3P seller services line and then 3P unit slow down, you might suggest that the third-party GMV expansion may not be happening quite as fast.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: So maybe just talk a little bit of that.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: Is this just law of large numbers as time goes by?

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: What is Amazon doing to sort of sustain that growth rate in the third-party marketplace business?

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: And then second question is maybe just quickly on media spend.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: Just update us on how you're thinking about the trajectory of video content spend.

speaker: Anthony DiClemente
sentence: Any strategic changes there in terms of library versus originals versus films or TV content?

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Let's step back on the third-party question.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So again, let me reiterate our approach.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So main goal here is to allow customers to have the broadest selection at the best available price and also the most convenient options on how they receive the item.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: If we're delivering on those three elements, we're indifferent as to whether it's sold by us or a third-party.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We actively recruit sellers to sell on our platform.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: It's because it adds selection, it's adds -- if it's in the FBA program, it adds Prime eligible selection and we spend billions of dollars a year, as Jeff said, on infrastructure tools and services, not only to allow sellers to sell, but to help them sell more successfully.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So we have a vested interest in the success of our sellers.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: Any growth acceleration or deceleration that you see can be very much tied to the total sales of the customer that we have the customers in any country.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So you'll still see the percentage of third-party units increased and has been steadily over the last few years.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: So again, the sellers are as important to us as anything for servicing the customers' need for price selection and convenience.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: The elements I just talked about of investment -- further investment in one-day shipping is directly going to be a cost that we bear and it's also going to be a direct benefit to sellers as well Prime eligible selection in our warehouses.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Anthony, just real quick, this is Dave on your question around media and probably more particularly the video strategy and what we're investing in.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: I mean, we're continuing to invest meaningfully in digital video.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: It's an area we're very excited about.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Lots of very popular critically acclaimed shows have obviously come out, things like Homecoming, Jack Ryan, more recently Hanna or Guava Island and some great titles.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So I think look for us to continue to invest there.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: There was -- on the accounting side, we did adopt an accounting standard in January that amended our accounting for how we how we cap produced original video content.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: And under that new guidance, we capitalized production cost for original video content.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Previously, we only capitalized a portion of those costs.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So -- the net impact for the first quarter to operating income wasn't material.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: It was -- for Q1, the impact of a change was a decrease of about $130 million to cost of sales due to the capitalization change.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: As we go through 2019 though, we would expect the impact to increase in the latter part of the second half of the year in line with our production schedule as it grows throughout the year.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Operator Our next question is from John Blackledge from Cowen and Company.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: You are now live.

sentence: Just coming back to the Prime one-day delivery.

sentence: Will it be available to most of the US by the holidays or by the end of the year?

sentence: So yes, on the one-day free shipping versus the two-day free shipping, our goal is to evolve the two-day ship -- free shipping program into a one-day free shipping program and we're making strides on that.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: It got into a little bit about the capacity we have to add and the changes we have to make to our supply chain in order to deliver on that.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We expect to make steady progress quickly and through the year.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We'll have more for you at the end of Q2, obviously.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: There's a lot of error bars around this program, especially from the cost side.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: We are -- felt we're doing something very important for the customer.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And we have -- again, trying to take advantage of the fulfillment capacity and transportation capacity, especially with third-party partners that we have.

speaker: Brian T. Olsavsky
sentence: And then we'll just have to see what changes have to be made to get more and more selection into that one-day category.

sentence: And then, this is Dave again, just on the grocery side of it.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: As you mentioned, Brian talked a bit about the Whole Foods Market growth over 500 stores, 75 metros with delivery capability, so continuing to grow that out.

sentence: We are also continuing to invest in our other grocery initiatives.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Amazon Fresh, Prime Now which offers grocery as one of the components of the selection there for the two-hour or even one-hour delivery capabilities.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: And so I think we'll keep investing in those areas.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: I mean -- and then in other initiatives as well, where we can get food through Pantry, Go, there's a number of initiatives there.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: So excited about what we'll be able to continue to bring to customers on that space.

speaker: Dave Fildes
sentence: Operator Our next question is from Ben Schachter from Macquarie Group.

sentence: You are now live.

sentence: So more on the one-day shipping.

sentence: Again, e-commerce sales in the third quarter ex FX increased 38.2% year over year.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Stronger departments included jewelry, home furnishings, sporting goods, hardware, and majors, which, of course, includes both everything from appliances to consumer electronics.

sentence: In terms of Costco Logistics and an update there, we anniversary-ed the purchase of Innovel, now called Costco Logistics this fiscal quarter.

sentence: Overall, we've improved delivery time on many items from up to two weeks to in many -- in several cases, now five to seven days.

sentence: As well, we've taken several items that were previously vendor-drop shipped and are now being direct imported allowing us to not only speed up delivery but reduce prices to our members.

sentence: From a supply chain perspective, port delays are continuing to have an impact.

sentence: We are utilizing additional carriers, in some cases, to help alleviate some of that.

sentence: Containers and pallets are also facing shortages anecdotally, 35% to 50% increase in incoming containers this year versus a year ago.

sentence: The turnaround of a container hitting the U.S., delivering its contents, and being back at the U.S. port to head back overseas has gone from approximately 25 days to 50 days.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Chips shortages are impacting many items from an inflation standpoint, some items more than others.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: And again, as I mentioned, with regard to containers and shipping, transportation costs have increased as well.

sentence: Despite these issues, we continue to work to mitigate cost increases and supply chain delays in a variety of different ways as best we can.

sentence: The biggest way we've handled supply chain delays is adjusted ordering and front-loading, if you will, orders of many items.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: And we think we've got that pretty well under control.

sentence: We've had a lot of questions about inflation over the past few months.

sentence: There have been and are a variety of inflationary pressures that we and others are seeing.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Inflationary factors abound.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: These include higher labor costs, higher freight costs, higher transportation demand, along with the container shortage and port delays that I mentioned, increased demand in various product categories some shortages, various shortages of everything from chips to oils and chemical supplies by facilities hit by the Gulf freeze and storms and, in some cases, higher commodity prices.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Some inflationary sound bites if you will.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Price increases on items shipped across the ocean with suppliers paying up to double for containers and shipping.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Price increases of pulp, paper goods, some things up 4% to 8%, plastic and resin increases from trash bags to plastic cups, plates, etc.,

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: and plastic wraps.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Metals, aluminum foil, mid-single-digit cost increases also cans for sodas and other beverages.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Higher import prices on cheeses, the combination of the product itself, as well as some FX strength of some foreign currencies, as well as freight, anywhere from 3% to 10% increases on certain apparel items, not all.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: In terms of fresh, higher protein prices, for example, meat overall year over year is up 7%.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Beef in the last month has been up as much as 20%.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Some of that is due to feed labor and transportation costs, as well as restocking some of the additional increased demand coming now from institutional needs as restaurants start to reopen.

sentence: And the list could go on and on.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: Now, all this being said, I was asked back on our March 4 second-quarter call.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: At what level we felt inflation was running overall at that time with our goods.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: I stated that our best guess was somewhere in the 1% to 1.5% range.

speaker: Richard Galanti

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: And some items are even down a little bit.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: We think, again, we've done pretty well in terms of controlling that as best as we can, but the inflation pressures abound.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: In terms of sampling and demos in the warehouse, as you all know, we eliminated our popular food sampling and demo activities in our warehouses last March at the onset of the pandemic.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: As various states opened and closed last summer and fall, we tried a few sampling events.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: A few single-serve items like cookies and crackers, take-out only, no-cook to prepared sample items, and a few enhanced talking demos such as items for display only.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: I'm happy to report that over the next couple of weeks, we're beginning a phased return to full sampling.

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: This will come in waves.

sentence: The first wave of locations, about 170 of our 550-ish locations in the U.S. will be activated by the first week of June, with most of the remaining locations returning toward the near -- or toward the end of June.

speaker: Richard Galanti

speaker: Richard Galanti
sentence: I'm sure there will be a few states with unique restrictions as well.

sentence: Increased safety protocols are and will be in place, including all samples prepared behind plexiglass, prepared in smaller batches for better safety control, and distribute it to members one at a time.

speaker: Richard Galanti

sentence: I'm pleased to report that our food courts are also coming back over the next few weeks in a bigger way.

sentence: Last March, again, in 2020 as the pandemic took hold, we pared back menu basically to hotdogs and pizza and soda and smoothies, and we eliminated all seating, those takeout-only.

sentence: And by June 7, we plan to have tables in seating back at most locations, but with more physical separation, tables of four instead of six and eight, and about half the seating capacity as we had before.

speaker: Richard Galanti

sentence: Look, there's a couple of things that I think are important to recognize.

sentence: Number one, not only have we transitioned over the last few years into what I would describe as a structurally lower ongoing capital program.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: But number two, it contains a much greater degree of flexibility.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: And we mentioned we pulled spending down 35% really over just nine months last year because we could flex that downward.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: And so we have a great degree of flexibility.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: We've got a high degree of capital efficiency in our portfolio.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: And even at these further reduced levels of spending, as Pierre mentioned, production will be somewhere between flat and up 3%.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: So we've got a capital program that we like.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: And as the TCO project comes down, we've got room to make choices.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: When we issued the press release, certainly, the Permian and the Gulf of Mexico would have been some of the first places to draw that capital back.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: As we look at some of the announcements of this week and developments that seem to be unfolding here in the U.S., it's early days to understand exactly how these will play out.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: The executive order was sweeping and broad, but it also lack some specificity.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: And I think, certainly, as you listen to some of the members of the new administration comment, as they introduce this and answered some questions, I think they're looking to flesh out the details here in the coming weeks and months.

speaker: Mike Wirth

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: Onshore in the Permian, we're weighted toward Texas more so than New Mexico.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: We're weighted toward private land more so than federal land.

speaker: Mike Wirth
sentence: So we've got a fair degree of flexibility there, and that remains a highly attractive place for us to step capital up as we have the capacity to do so and the market conditions support it.

sentence: If conditions in the U.S. become so onerous that it really disincentivizes investment, we've got other places where we can take those dollars.

sentence: That makes a lot of sense.

sentence: So quickly, I'll reiterate that last year, we completed all module fabrication and all the transportation to get the modules through the Russian inland waterway systems through the Caspian unloaded into site.

sentence: That's a really important milestone because those were risks that could have extended things had we not accomplished that.

sentence: And as Pierre said, we've remobilized 20,000 workers to the project.

sentence: We've plateaued at that number now because Tengiz is experiencing some of the same winter time uptick in coronavirus cases as you're seeing around the world.

speaker: Mike Wirth
