sentence: A near '21 question, then I have a follow-up on a longer-term question.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: In the SG&A outlook, on our math, you have about a billion dollars related to COVID costs, such as special bonuses and cleaning, as well your raise to $15 an hour midyear.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: To what extent are you assuming these costs are tailwinds in '21, and can you quantify how significant the operating expense is related to investment that's pressuring SG&A dollars?

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: I can take that one, Chris.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: When you think about -- within the year, we'll be annualizing the move to $15, and there will be some one-time things that don't repeat.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Just think about buying Plexiglas dividers, you only do that once.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: The final story in SG&A will be written by what our sales outcome looks like too, but we've got a lot of leverage within the model to continue to bend the cost curves in a direction we like throughout SG&A. The benefit of the volume growth that we've seen is that that helps us get more and more efficient on how we fulfill that volume.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: So then does it mean that the SG&A rate coming back up is more about an embedded negative top-line outlook?

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: I wouldn't think about it that way necessarily.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: With SG&A, we expect that our SG&A rate will be lower than 2019's rate, and that's a benefit of the significant scale that we've gained since then.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: If you zoom out, I think there's going to be a lot of movement between the different levers within the margin and SG&A, and so that's why we've tried to give some of our best thinking on the operating rate in total.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: It's a wide range.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Not every meeting I would herein be describing a one-point gap in operating margin between the incredibly strong 6 that we had in 2019 and the seven we just put up.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: That whole range is in play.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: I think it's slightly more likely we're in the bottom half of that range when all the dust settles than the top half, but we're going to have a lot to learn throughout the year based on where we ultimately land.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Then longer term and bigger picture, you've talked about showrooming with Best Buy.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Was wondering what the organizational thought change on showrooming is versus national brands.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: You launched Apple and now you have Ulta.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: What's the thought change here, and what does it say the willingness to take on more national brands in the apparel space, where maybe the brands need to replace volumes from the mall and is the bar higher here in terms of what those brands will need to bring to get into the Target store?

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I think one of the things that we underscored throughout the pandemic has been the strength of our stores, and despite many Americans really avoiding public places, we've seen very strong store comps, obviously in excess of 7%, and we saw very solid store traffic, so I think we've continued to build trust and I think coming out of the pandemic, our stores are going to continue to be very relevant, very important.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I think they go far beyond showcasing.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We know our guests are inspired by shopping at our stores.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: They enjoy browsing, they enjoy seeing the combination of our own brands and national brands, and now I think we just punctuate that further with the addition of brands like Ulta Beauty, Levi's, the expansion of Apple, the work that we've done throughout the year to create a showcase of own brands and national brands, and continue to invest in building a trusted and safe shopping experience.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: As we think to the future, stores are going to play a very important role.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: It's going to be a place where our guests enjoy shopping each and every day, and I think they're going to continue to enjoy our multi-category portfolio for years to come.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We continue to be very bullish on the role stores play, and I think these new national brand partnerships will only accentuate the importance of stores and drive future traffic to our stores.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Thanks, and best of luck.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: The biggest factor versus a couple of years ago on the SG&A line is going to be the benefit of scale, and we can put that to use in so many ways across the business.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: We've got a long history of investing in our team.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: That was a big part of the journey we embarked on in 2017, attracting and retaining the best team in retail has been a center of our strategy for the last several years and we continue to put the team at the forefront this year, and that will continue as well.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Karen, I might as well take the guidance question upfront and kind of remove the bull's eye from Michael's chest.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Again, no pun intended, but as we sit here today, I think we all recognize this is a very uncertain environment.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We're still speculating around what's going to happen with the economy, how employment rates start to recover.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: While the trends are encouraging right now with the virus, we're all battling COVID each and every day, and while vaccine distribution is accelerating, millions and millions of Americans are still waiting for their turn to get that vaccine.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We're still wondering when children go back to school and when we'll return to the workplace, so we approach guidance recognizing there is lots of uncertainty.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: But I'll go back to the fact that for most of the last year, we haven't provided guidance but we have focused on execution, and I think our team has proven to be very flexible, very agile.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We've responded to the environment and we've been focused on delivering a trusted and safe experience for our guests, whether they're shopping at our stores or online.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: That focus on execution will continue in 2021 and I wouldn't confuse guidance or the lack thereof with our confidence to continue to take market share and outperform in the coming months and years.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I recognize the frustration of not being more precise, particularly on the top line as we think about sales, but I can guarantee you our entire leadership team and every part of this organization is focused on retaining and growing market share, no matter what the variables are we have to face.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I recognize that we'd certainly like to be in a different position today, providing more precision, but what I can tell you is we're going to continue to execute our strategy, leverage our capabilities, our own brands and national brands, our multi-category assortment, and our team to continue to build on the momentum we gained in 2020, leverage the additional $15 billion of revenue we now have inside of our P&L, and continue to build on the market share we gained in 2020 and make sure that's very sticky for years to come.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: But I recognize for all of you, you'd love more precision around the market share, you'd love some more top-line insights.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I can tell you, we're off to a very strong start in February; in fact, our comps in February started with a two handle, and that's a 20 comp in the first part of the year, so we'll see how that plays out in March and April, but we're off to a strong start.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We took significant market share in the fourth quarter.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: If you recall our comments in earlier meetings, we talked about the fact that in the first three quarters of the year, we had picked up approximately $6 billion of market share, but we added another $3 billion of market share during the holiday season where all of our competitors were operating, so I think the vibrancy of our model, our ability to execute is something that I would ask all of you to focus in on, and I recognize you've got to do that in light of the fact that we haven't provided the precision that we normally do at this time.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Appreciate that.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Thank you very much.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: I just wanted to ask a bigger picture question.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: With respect to the partnerships that you've announced, what is the gating factor on accelerating or not accelerating some of these partnerships at a faster rate?

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: I mean, you've obviously given us the number of remodels that you've done and I'm sure they're not all primary targets for some of these partnerships, but it seems like you could move a little faster on those, so a little color on that would be great.

sentence: Karen, I'll go back over time and think about the work we've been doing for the last five or six years.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We always start by testing and learning, listening to the guests, listening to our team, iterating along the way, validating our assumptions both from a sales standpoint and a financial standpoint before we accelerate.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: This is the same approach we've taken with remodels over the years and new small formats.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: It's the same approach we took to pick-up and drive-up, and we're doing the same thing as we think about partnerships with great partners, like Apple and Ulta Beauty.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We want to test and learn, make sure we get the model right, and then as we've demonstrated in the past, we'll hit the accelerator and make sure we expand and leverage scale as quickly as possible.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Thanks very much, and congratulations on a great year.

sentence: So biggest driver in 2021 for sure, and I would welcome more digital growth going forward and we expect that's a place where we'll continue to excel.

sentence: They gained market share, very strong results for the business serving our retail partners, and just as important, and I'll come back to this, is Shipt has become an integral part of Target and our fulfillment and same-day operations, so incredibly important there.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: But I think the team down in Birmingham did an outstanding job this year just scaling the business.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: They doubled the number of shoppers.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: We talked about how the Target sales on Shipt grew by 300%.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: Memberships grew by 130%.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: We continue to add great retail partners like Best Buy and Bed, Bath and Beyond, and several and local and regional grocers, and so they've done just a really great job continuing to scale that business.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: I think when it comes to Shipt and obviously the relationship with Target, incredibly important part about our same-day options.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: You heard us talk all morning today about the key lever, that having that suite of fulfillment, same-day fulfillment options for our Target guests has been over the past year, and really over the past several years, and will continue to be in the future.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: Not only is that the preferred way our guest continues to grow with us, but they're also economically advantaged, and so we continue to see huge opportunities for Shipt to continue to work directly with Target to continue to fulfill our guests' needs.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: The other thing I would say is we see -- very similar to drive-up, when a guest engages with Shipt through Target, again we see growth in our sales in-store and online on the Target platform as well, so they get more engaged with Target.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: That is hugely valuable for us.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: We bought that capability three years ago thinking this is what it would be.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: It would be incredibly important for us from a same-day perspective.

speaker: John Mulligan
sentence: It has only become more so as that accelerated through 2020.

sentence: I'd just go back to a point that we've made a number of times.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Our most valuable guest is the guest that utilizes all of our assets, shops in our stores, leverages order pick-up, uses drive-up when it's convenient for them, and also more and more leverages the benefit of a personal shopper through Shipt, so we think that continues to be the easiest place to shop in America.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Having all those assets available for our guests is critically important, and we think those are going to be very sticky over time.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Those guests who utilize drive-up and Shipt during the pandemic, we think there's going to be a lasting connection to those fulfillment options as we go forward in 2021 and beyond.

sentence: Ed, I'll go back to the commitment we made at this meeting in 2017, when John Mulligan and I laid out our strategy for the company and talked about the billions of dollars of capital we'd invest in stores, in remodeling stores, and building new stores, and building out our digital and fulfillment capabilities.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: At that time, we said the most important investment we were making was in our team, and I think the results we've seen in 2017 and 2018 and 2019, and 2020 is a byproduct of that commitment to our team, investing in wages and benefits, investing in training and crew opportunities, and I think it's allowed us to build the best team in retail, that's incredibly engaged, that's focused on taking care of our guests, but also taking care of each other.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Our team was really the star of 2020.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: They stepped up during the pandemic and made sure we created a safe shopping environment.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: As we scaled drive-up and saw growth rates of 500% or 600%, they flexed and were able to meet the needs of the guests, so I think the fact that we've taken a leadership position with wages, invested in our team, provided them the opportunities to grow their careers, that's a hallmark of the commitment we've made at Target to creating the best team in retail.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I think it's provided great returns on investments for shareholders.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We'll continue to make sure we invest in our team.

sentence: To your question around design, the investments we've made in food and beverage, Good and Gather is off to a tremendous start, a multi-billion dollar brand in a short period of time.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: It's been well received by our guests, great quality at a great value, and I think it typifies the things we do with our own brands.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We're very excited about the momentum we have in food and beverage.

speaker: Brian Cornell

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: As John mentioned, we'll continue to add fresh products to our drive-up assortment and pick-up assortment throughout the year, providing our guests access to more of those products that they're looking for each and every day.

sentence: Within the quarter, May saw the smallest increase this year, given that it was comping over a 33% increase a year ago.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: On a two-year basis, results were much more consistent throughout the quarter as we saw two-year growth in excess of 30% across all three months.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As Brian mentioned, with guests spending more time out of their homes, we've seen them shopping more often and making slightly smaller trips.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Specifically, traffic grew 12.7% in the second quarter, partially offset by a 3.4% decline in average ticket.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: However, given that last year's comp growth was primarily driven by average ticket, on a two-year basis, we've seen double-digit increases in both traffic and ticket since 2019.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As Brian also mentioned, the store channel has been our primary growth driver this year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Specifically, store comparable sales grew 8.7% in the second quarter.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And given that store comps increased 10.9% last year, we've seen compounded growth of our in-store sales of more than 20% over the last two years.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: In the digital channel, comp sales grew 10% on top of 195% a year ago.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And reflecting this year's change in guests' shopping habits, the mix of our digital fulfillment changed meaningfully.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Specifically, same-day services grew 55% in the quarter, while sales on orders shipped to home actually declined from last year's elevated levels.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This provides vivid evidence of the stickiness of our same-day services.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Once guests try them, they love them.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: So even as they've ramped up their in-store shopping, they've continued to rely on these services as well.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Another indication of this year's shift in guest behavior, the percent of total sales from the digital channel actually fell slightly compared with last year, moving from 17.2% in second-quarter 2020 back to 17% this year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Obviously, this isn't a trend we expect will continue over time, and it's important to note that this year's digital penetration of 17% is well over double the 7.3% we reported in second-quarter 2019.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Our second-quarter gross margin rate of 30.4% was down about 50 basis points from 30.9% a year ago.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Among the drivers, last year's change in the sales return reserve estimate, which contributed about $110 million to second-quarter gross margin last year, accounted for about 50 basis points of rate pressure this year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: In other words, without last year's benefit from this change in the reserve estimate, our second-quarter gross margin rate would have been about flat compared to last year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Among other gross margin drivers, we saw about 70 basis points of pressure in merchandising, reflecting the impact of higher product and freight costs, partially offset by the benefit of low markdown rates.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This pressure was offset by about 40 basis points of tailwind for merchandise mix, combined with a small benefit from supply chain and digital fulfillment, driven by the shift in digital mix toward our less costly same-day options.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: On the SG&A expense line, we saw a rate of 19.3% this year, down about 10 basis points from last year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This change reflected the continued leverage benefit from strong sales growth, offset by pressure from an increase in some expense rates in areas like marketing from lower-than-normal levels a year ago.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This year's SG&A expenses also reflect continued growth in pay and benefits for our team.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: On the D&A line, we saw about 20 basis points of rate improvement from last year, driven by leverage on our sales growth.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Altogether, second-quarter operating margin rate was 9.8%, down about 20 basis points from a year ago but more than 2.5 percentage points higher than second-quarter 2019.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: On the bottom line, our second-quarter GAAP EPS of $3.65 was 8.9% higher than a year ago, and adjusted EPS of $3.64 was 7.9% above last year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Second-quarter GAAP and adjusted EPS have both doubled over the last two years.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: So far, this year, our operations have generated just over $3.4 billion of cash.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This is historically strong performance, but about $1.7 billion lower than a year ago due to some unique circumstances affecting last year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Specifically, our inventory position at the end of the second quarter last year was much lower than we'd have preferred given that our sales had far outpaced our expectations during the first half of the year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As a result, at this point last year, inventory turnover and payables leverage were running unusually high and would have been lower had we owned the appropriate amount of inventory to support our sales.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As such, this year, our inventory is in a much better position, more than $2 billion higher than last year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And our payables leverage has begun to decline to a more sustainable level, both of which are near-term headwinds to operating cash flow.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: In addition, our year-to-date income tax payments are more than $1 billion higher than at this time last year, given the volatility in our taxable income through the first half of last year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As I turn to capital deployment, I want to start where I always do, which is to reiterate our priorities, which have remained the same for decades.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: First, we invest fully in our business in projects that meet our strategic and financial criteria.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Then we look to support the dividend and build on our record of annual dividend increases, which we've maintained every year since 1971.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And finally, we return any excess cash over time through share repurchases within the limits of our strong middle A credit ratings.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: So far, this year, we've invested just over $1.3 billion in capex to support the new store, remodel, and supply chain projects that John outlined earlier.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And for the year, we're now expecting capex in the $3.5 billion range.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This is about $0.5 billion lower than our original expectation and reflects the retiming of some project spending into next year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As a result of this retiming, our view of next year's capex is somewhat higher than our prior view, in the $4 billion to $5 billion range.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And we'll continue to refine our view as we move into next year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Bottom line, we're excited about the productive opportunities in front of us, and we'll govern our investment decisions with a focus on delivering continued growth and superior returns.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Beyond our capital investments, we paid dividends of $336 million in the second quarter, and we returned another $1.5 billion through share repurchases at an average price of just over $230.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And as we announced today, our board has approved a new $15 billion share repurchase authorization, which will allow us to continue buying back shares once the current $5 billion program is completed.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This authorization is consistent with the capital deployment priorities I outlined above.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: It also reflects our confidence in the ongoing strength of our business and the robust cash flow we expect to generate over time.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Even after this year's investments in our business and team and the return of capital to our shareholders, we ended the second quarter with cash and cash equivalents of about $7.4 billion.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This is up slightly from a year ago and well above the cash position we expect to maintain over time.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: But as I've said before, given our current cash position and elevated volatility in the current environment, we believe it will be a multiyear journey before our exceptionally strong cash and credit metrics move fully back to long-term levels consistent with our single A credit ratings.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Before I turn to our expectations, I want to close my review of our current performance with a brief discussion of our after-tax return on invested capital, which measures the performance of our investment decisions over time.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: For the trailing 12 months through the end of the second quarter, Target's after-tax ROIC was 31.7%, compared with 17.2% a year ago.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This is an amazing number and a testament to the performance of our business model and our team over the last year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As we've said before, we expect this metric could settle back into the mid to high 20s over time, but to deliver a sustainable after-tax return in that range is a remarkable performance in any industry.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And these superior returns are one of the many reasons we're eager to continue investing in the growth and resilience of our business to the benefit of all of our stakeholders.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Now let's turn to our comp sales expectations for the fall season.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: As you'll recall, in our conference call 90 days ago, we described how our business was positioned to deliver single-digit comp growth in the back half of the year, on top of very strong growth of more than 20% in the back half of 2020.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: While the environment remains volatile today, and there are many uncertainties as we look ahead, Target's performance through the first half of the year has consistently exceeded our expectations.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: This performance, combined with the continued strength in the U.S. consumer, gives us increasing confidence that this fall, our business can generate comparable sales growth in the high single-digit range, near the high end of our previous guidance range.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: We have a similar outlook regarding profitability.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: 90 days ago, we said we expected our full-year operating margin rate would be well above the 2020 rate of 7%, with a potential for it to reach 8% or somewhat higher.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: From today's perspective, based on our expectation of high single-digit comp growth in the fall, we expect to see an operating margin rate near the high end of our previous range.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Specifically, we now believe that Target is positioned to deliver an operating margin rate of 8% or higher for the full year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: I've been at Target for more than 17 years now, and I've never experienced a time like this when every aspect of our diverse strategy is coming together like we're seeing today.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Obviously, our guests are noticing, too, based on their higher level of engagement, which you can see in our outstanding performance.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Typically, in retail, if you saw a large, mature company like ours growing at the rate we're seeing today, you'd assume we were comping over soft numbers from the prior year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Instead, we're comping over a year of record growth in 2020 on both the top and bottom lines.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Like Brian said earlier, our success begins and ends with the team.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: So on behalf of all of our stakeholders, I'd like to close my remarks today by thanking the entire Target team for the exceptional results we're reporting today.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Now I'll turn the call back over to Brian.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Thanks, Michael.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Before we move to your questions, I want to pick up on Michael's last point, which is the way we've been able to synchronize every aspect of our strategy.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: A few years ago, we embarked on a project to better articulate our company purpose.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Across our team, there was already a strong sense of who we are and what we stand for, but we wanted to put it into words distinctly.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Out of that work came the purpose we articulate today: to help all families discover the joy of everyday life.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Those words have deep meaning for our team: families, discovery, joy, and the word all, which represents our strong commitment to inclusion across every aspect of our business.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Some might ask if everyone at Target already had a strong sense of purpose, why go to the trouble of putting it into words?

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: The answer is the alignment that it creates, alignment of our strategy, and alignment of our team.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: In the same way we had a focus on what really matters most in our articulation of our purpose, we're relying on that purpose to focus both our strategic work and our everyday activities.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: If we find ourselves working on something that doesn't advance our purpose, we can set it aside and relentlessly focus on the things that will move Target forward.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: That kind of focus has enabled the performance we're reporting today, and it's behind all of our investments, strategies, and activities as we look ahead.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: With that, let's move to Q&A. Christina, John, Michael, and I will be happy to take your questions.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Good morning, everybody.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: So two questions.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: My first question is, can you talk about what you're seeing in back-to-school so far?

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Are you seeing any effect from Delta on purchasing patterns?

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: And how are you thinking about growth in the different categories as you move forward relative to the second quarter?

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Chris, we're off to a really strong back-to-school start, and it is broad-based right now.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Christina and Michael, John, and I were out in stores yesterday, and we were seeing guests shopping our entire back-to-school assortment.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I think we've got a great assortment at a tremendous value, and we're off to a really strong back-to-school and back-to-college season.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: And then a follow-up, Mike, on the gross margin.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Can you talk about how you're thinking about the gross margin in the back half overall?

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: And within that, what are the puts and takes?

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Does that -- do the product and freight headwinds persist or perhaps elevate?

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: And to what degree are you assuming higher clearance and promotion levels to drive the 8% or more operating margin outlook?

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Chris, you've heard us talk over time about all the levers we have within the business to offset some of those puts and takes.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And I think the second quarter is a really good example of that.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: If you take out the sales return adjustment in last year's actuals, margins were essentially flat year over year.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And so we found some good offsets there and feel really good about our profit performance.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: I actually think that same theme comes through loud and clear if we zoom out a little bit and look at a longer time period.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: If you go back to first half of this year versus first half of 2019, 2019 gross margin rate was 30.1% for the Q1 and Q2 season.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: We're sitting at 30.4% right now in Q2 and 30.2% for the spring.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And so a lot's happened over the last two years, and we feel really good about our ability to manage the profitability of the business.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And I think that bodes well for the back half of this year and beyond.

speaker: Chris Horvers
sentence: Thanks very much, and best of luck.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: The next question is from Paul Lejuez with Citi.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: You may go ahead.

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: Just curious on the inflation front, if you can maybe talk about the cost pressures that you're seeing in the food grocery category versus general merchandise, any quantification that you might be able to provide.

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: And also wanted to go back to private label performance.

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: You mentioned it grew faster in 2Q. Curious what sort of the gross margin tailwind that provided.

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: And how do you see private label performance playing out in the second half?

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: Is that going to be a continued gross margin driver for you?

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Well, let's have Christina talk about the strength we're seeing in our owned brand performance and how we're managing costs in this environment.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: Good morning, Paul.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: I'd be happy to take that one.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: Let's start with owned brands.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: As you know, owned brands are a huge part of our strategic imperative and desire to continue to differentiate in the market, bring great quality products to our guests.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: And so our commitment is to continue to accelerate our owned brands at a faster rate than our base, and that is what exactly what we saw in the second quarter.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: That's the pattern we've been on.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: And as long as we continue to find unique opportunities to meet the guests' needs, that's going to persist.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: And so you also know that owned brands represent a big portion of our sales mix, but even a bigger portion of our gross margin.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: So that creates tailwind for us on the profit side.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: And then going back to your first question on costs, yes, we're seeing cost pressures on product costs, as well as freight.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: But going back to Michael's point, this is what we do every day.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: We manage the profitability of the business by leveraging the full suite of levers that we have to offer great value to our guests while delivering on the financial expectations you have.

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: The next question is from Karen Short with Barclays.

speaker: Paul Lejuez
sentence: You may go ahead.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Thanks very much.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: So I wanted to just ask, you look at your sales productivity, you're up more than 40% on a sales per square foot basis since 2017.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: So I guess what I'm wondering is, with this higher productivity, how should we think about kind of the long-term margin structure?

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Or maybe said a little differently, would you look to lean into investments going forward?

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Or could we expect a little more sustainability in terms of the higher operating margin structure?

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: If I step back from your question a little bit, Karen, at the end of the day, growth powers so much of our margin equation.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And that's why we're so focused on investments that drive growth.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And you can certainly see that in the improved productivity.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: That comes to bear.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And the math we do on new stores, that comes to bear for how we adjust our store footprint in a remodel.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And so you'll see us consistently focused on investments that drive growth.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: With that growth comes good productivity on a per square foot basis, and we can translate that growth to good bottom-line profit.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Karen, Michael summarized it well.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: I mean, our theme for this quarter was growth on top of growth.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: But you should expect that theme to continue going forward.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We're going to continue to invest in our stores.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: John talked about the remodel plans that we have in place.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We'll continue to invest in new, highly productive stores, invest in our brands, invest in our fulfillment services, and invest in our team.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And our focus on continuing to drive consistent growth and market share expansion quarter after quarter will be a theme you'll hear for years to come.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Thanks for that.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: And then just you also commented on the 70 basis points of gross margin pressure from higher product and freight costs.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: On the product front, can you maybe just give a little color on what you're seeing on the cost inflation versus the retail inflation?

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: And are you absorbing some of that cost inflation?

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: I think Christina said it well, our teams are experts at managing the puts and takes across the business.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: So if we rewind the clock a couple of years ago, we'll be talking about tariffs and how we offset that.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And I feel really good about how our teams manage any complexity in the business.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: To underscore something Christina also said, value matters, and we'll be laser-focused on making sure our guests find incredible value on our site and in our stores.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And so we've done a lot of hard work to invest in solid price perception.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And we want to make sure that our guests continue to find that value going forward, inflation or not.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: The next question is from Scott Mushkin with R5 Capital.

speaker: Karen Short
sentence: You may go ahead.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: Hey, guys, thanks for taking my questions.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: I guess the first one I have is, obviously, you're holding a lot of cash on your balance sheet.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: You guys talked about the new share repurchase.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: But what is the ideal level of cash for you guys to hold?

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: And what do you do with what you got now, I guess, in more of the short term?

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Well, the answer to that question, priority 1 has been and always will be invest in the business.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And continuing to invest to drive growth is the first use of that cash.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Our second capital priority is to support the dividend.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: We announced just last month a north of 30% increase in our per-share dividend.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And we have the good fortune of a business that continues to generate a lot of cash as we grow.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And so that gives us capacity for share repurchase as well.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Over time, you'll see us carry less cash than that $7.4 billion we have today to be sure.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: Optimal and normal times, it's something closer to flat to a little north of that cash on the balance sheet, depending on the period of the year we're in.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: But we want to be prudent about how we kind of step back into the sweet spot of our middle A credit ratings.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: And then my second question is really, I guess, more strategic over the next 12 to 18 months.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: Brian, I think you went over just what tremendous work the team has done.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: But if you step back and look at the next 12 to 18 months, what are the biggest, I guess, initiatives going forward that would drive outsized growth, that market share gain compared to competitors?

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Scott, it will be a very familiar theme to you.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We're going to continue to invest in remodeling our stores.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And despite the progress we've made, and we've remodeled just about half our stores today.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: So you'll continue to see us invest in remodels.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We've got a very strong pipeline of new stores that we'll be rolling out over the next few years.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We'll continue to invest in our brands and our owned brand performance.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: You'll continue to see us continue to invest in Drive Up and pickup and the expansion of Shipt.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And we'll continue to invest in our team, again, all built around that thematic of growth.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And as we think about the key metrics going forward, you'll hear us talk about traffic, and we felt exceptionally good this quarter about driving traffic growth of almost 13%, continue to drive strong comps in both our stores and digital channels.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And we'll continue to make sure we always are laser-focused on market share gains.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: So those themes will be very consistent going forward.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: The investments we make in our stores, our brands, our fulfillment channels, and our team will continue to drive traffic to our stores and visits to our site, continue to drive strong comps that equate to market share gains across our entire portfolio.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: So that's our continued commitment for not just the next few quarters but for years to come.

speaker: Scott Mushkin
sentence: And what a tremendous job you guys have done.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: Operator Thank you.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: The next question is from Michael Lasser with UBS.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: You may go ahead.

speaker: Michael Lasser
sentence: Thanks for taking my question.

speaker: Michael Lasser
sentence: Target continues to see outsized gains in traffic.

speaker: Michael Lasser
sentence: Over the last 90 days, has there been any change in the nature of the pattern of traffic, more weekly traffic versus weekend, especially as consumers go out and travel and do other activities?

speaker: Michael Lasser
sentence: And how are you expecting your traffic to unfold over the next couple of quarters as you guide to high single digits for the back half of the year?

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: Michael, maybe I can jump in on this one.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: Traffic has been very consistent, and it's been consistently strong.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: And we're very excited about the early momentum in back-to-school and back-to-college as well.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: What I would tell you is that the strength of our portfolio allows us to flex between patterns in consumer behavior changes that are more at the micro-level, not at the aggregate level.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: The aggregate has been consistent and healthy.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: But there are behavior changes within businesses.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: We've talked about the fact that last year, there was a bigger need for household essentials and people were stocking up.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: Now we're seeing less of that, and we're seeing more the return to going out.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: And therefore, they're wearing dresses and beauty products, and luggage business has been very strong.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: So there are patterns underneath, but the macro and aggregate is that Target is outpacing the industry.

speaker: Christina Hennington
sentence: And it's really led by broad-based strength across all of our businesses.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And, Michael, I would just come back to -- I know there's been lots of questions about the impact of the Delta variant.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And we watch this very carefully.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: We're obviously very focused on safety.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: But we continue to see a very optimistic consumer, certainly shopping with caution and they're wearing masks more and more across the country.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: But we're seeing tremendous resilience in the consumer today.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And our traffic patterns, I think, represent that, as we see this consistent flow of traffic into our stores.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: So a very resilient consumer.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: And we're seeing that as we start the third quarter.

speaker: Brian Cornell
sentence: That traffic pattern and that resilience is continuing.

speaker: Michael Lasser
sentence: My follow-up question is after a year and a half past the start of the pandemic, you've comped the comp, you've seen really sizable returns on the investments that you've made and you've entered into a stable operating rhythm.

speaker: Michael Lasser
sentence: So why wouldn't Target now be able to sustain at least an 8% operating margin over the long run?

speaker: Michael Lasser
sentence: Is there something unique about this current environment such as a low level of promotional activity that might return in the future that would weigh on Target's profitability?

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: So, Michael, there's always something unique in the environment.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: I can't remember one of these calls where there wasn't a specific good guy or bad guy on the margin line we weren't talking about.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And so I think what matters most is our ability to put together a P&L that hangs together great, and that always starts with sales growth.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And so while we aren't in a position today to share a new algorithm, go forward, we'll be centered on continued sales growth and continued market share gains.

speaker: Michael Fiddelke
sentence: And with those, I'm confident in our team's ability to put together a P&L that translates into a bottom line we'll all feel good about.
